thought.text: process-compose is still alive with 8 services listening — my signals didn't take effect. Let me retry the teardown with explicit verification:

reasoning_content:
Even though I sent a signal, the process-compose process is still running, and 8 services are still listening (the 15 that were running from before). The podman error is probably caused by process-compose reacting to the SIGTERM it received: on shutdown, process-compose tries to stop its "containers" (it auto-detects docker/podman containers) — it tries to stop the containers that its process created… no wait, that's not it. process-compose has a feature where, on exit, it stops containers listed in the config, and in some versions it scans for docker containers and tries podman as a fallback too. The error text "Cannot connect to Podman" is coming out of process-compose's shutdown-time container cleanup.

Since the SIGTERM to process-compose (18011) apparently didn't fully stop it (or it got stuck on the podman cleanup), let me kill it more forcefully: KILL 18011 and 17988, then verify that all the child processes have been stopped.

Actually, wait — process-compose 18011 is still alive, and 8 services are listening. So that means the earlier `kill -TERM 18011` didn't work, or it got restarted… no, process-compose doesn't restart itself. Did the signal get intercepted? The podman error that was displayed might have been process-compose's response output (writing to stderr of the terminal session? No…).

Hmm, actually: I ran `kill -TERM 18011; sleep 10; kill -TERM 17988...` — but that command itself exited with a podman error (exit code 125). So the podman error text that appeared came from a process that shared the terminal session… the timeout wrapper kills its own child processes after the command completes. The podman error is…

Whatever — the current facts: process-compose 18011 is alive, 8 ports are listening, 34 service processes are alive. My signals didn't stop them. Let me verify whether the kill actually reached them: try again with explicit verification in a separate command.

action.command: kill -TERM 18011; echo "sent TERM to 18011, rc=$?"; sleep 8; kill -0 18011 2>/dev/null && echo "18011 STILL ALIVE" || echo "18011 gone"; kill -0 17988 2>/dev/null && echo "17988 STILL ALIVE" || echo "17988 gone"
